extracted.intended_audience: TeX implementers, macro-package authors, and advanced TeX users/programmers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and programming idioms for TeX character-code handling and advanced macro techniques, aimed at implementers and experienced macro writers to ensure portability, correctness, and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a standard internal code for portability
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX converts everything it reads to a standard internal code and converts back when writing files so the same results are produced on all machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes TeX constructions portable: e.g., alphabetic constants ('b) always denote the same integer so machine-independent macros can rely on fixed numeric values. The same internal code survives into dvi output so printing software that doesn't know the originating host gets essentially identical output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal code based on ASCII
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX's internal code is based on the American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII): 128 codes numbered 0–127 (octal '000–'177 or hexadecimal "00–"7F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 94 visible symbols are in standard ASCII; octal/hex equivalents are used in descriptions. Awareness of the standard ASCII assignments (control positions and visible symbols) is assumed when writing portable TeX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementations on large character sets should follow recommended mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: On systems with larger character sets, TeX implementations should be consistent with recommended code assignments (examples provided in the appendix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives an extended ASCII mapping developed at MIT (similar to Stanford's) and recommends that implementations on systems with many characters adhere to those suggested assignments to ease portability and user comfort (e.g., preserve useful extra characters such as arrows, slashes, tildes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro packages intended for wide use should stick to standard ASCII
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers of TeX macro packages that are intended to be widely used should stick to the standard ASCII characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid depending on extended charset characters in macro interfaces if macros will be widely distributed, because many users lack those characters on their keyboards or systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for systems with fewer than 95 externally representable symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: If a system has fewer than 95 symbols, a TeX implementer should follow explicit guidelines to preserve ASCII conventions and portability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: (a) stay as close as possible to ASCII conventions; (b) ensure codes '041–'046, '141–'146, and '160–'171 are present and that each unrepresentable internal code < '200 maps to a representable code when '100 is added/subtracted; (c) cooperate with others adopting the same policy. Plain TeX also provides control sequences (q,  lbrack, etc.) to substitute for missing characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: INITEX must initialize code tables identically
rubrics_metrics.description: INITEX initializes TeX's code tables as described (Appendix B), and the same initialization must be done by all implementations of TeX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent initialization across implementations is required so macros depending on initial catcodes/uccode/lccode etc. behave the same everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve syntax-character codes and keyword mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX uses specific characters (digits, punctuation, certain symbols and most letters) in its syntax and keywords; implementations must map keyboard characters so those syntactic codes and keyword spellings remain correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when implementing TeX for Cyrillic keyboards, assign Cyrillic letters to codes such that control word keywords (like pt) still have the expected code values, or else define control sequences so that TeX 'sees' the equivalent keywords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations must generate consistent character codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Commands like \number, \romannumeral, \the and \meaning generate letters, digits, spaces, decimal points, minus signs, double quotes, colons, and '>' signs; these should be the same codes in all implementations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macro and package code can rely on these commands producing a standardized set of character tokens across implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and pattern behavior must be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: The \hyphenation and \pattern commands give special interpretation to the ten digits and the characters '.' and '_' in patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementations should maintain the special treatment of these characters so patterns and hyphenation behave identically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special tokens inserted during error recovery have defined codes and catcodes
rubrics_metrics.description: When TeX recovers from certain errors, codes for four characters ($ . { }) are inserted and braces are inserted around an \output routine; appropriate catcodes are attached to those tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementations must ensure these inserted tokens and their catcodes are consistent so error recovery and consequent macro behavior are portable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hexadecimal representation convention for characters 0–255
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a convention for representing characters 0–255 in hexadecimal forms (..00–..ff); this convention is always acceptable as input when '..' is any character of catcode 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text output uses this convention only when representing characters a TeX installer has chosen not to output directly. Implementations should accept (and, where appropriate, produce) this hexadecimal representation consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified ASCII code-sets are nonstandard
rubrics_metrics.description: Any code sets obtained by modifying the standard ASCII assignments (or other arbitrary replacements) are nonstandard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on nonstandard replacements will reduce portability and should be avoided for widely distributed macros or implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven ASCII control characters occupy standard (hidden) positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven ASCII control characters (NUL, HT, LF, FF, CR, ESC, DEL) are conventionally assigned to ASCII positions and typically don't appear on keyboards; they exist as hidden characters appearing only on certain output devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macro writers should be aware that these 'hidden' characters behave specially and are not normally typed; implementations should place them at standard positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX represents characters internally as 0–255; input/output subsets may vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern TeX represents characters internally as numbers 0–255; implementations may differ in which characters they accept on input and which they will transmit on output, and these subsets can be specified independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A completely permissive implementation allows full 256-character input and output, but other versions may restrict to visible ASCII or make other choices. Macro and format authors must account for such variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, straightforward solutions before 'dirty tricks'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not read or apply the advanced 'dirty tricks' material until you have plenty of experience with plain TeX; try simple solutions first because usually a simpler and better way exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced, clever constructions may be inscrutable and harder to maintain; use them only when necessary and with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand expansion phases: expandable vs unexpandable (mouth vs stomach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control sequences are divided into expandable (macros, \if...\fi, special ops like \the and \input) and unexpandable (primitive commands); expansion occurs in TeX's 'mouth' while primitive assignments occur in the 'stomach'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include inability to redefine control sequences or advance a register while TeX is expanding a token list (e.g., in \message or \write). Macro authors must design around these phases and use appropriate techniques ( uturelet, \expandafter, \afterassignment) to get desired behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose macro construction for variable repetition with attention to complexity and resource limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple ways exist to construct a variable number of repeated tokens (example: producing \n asterisks); solutions differ in time complexity and resource use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple looped \xdef or token-list register constructions can be O(n^2); an \aftergroup-based construction is faster but consumes n input-stack and save-stack entries (may require special TeX for n>~150). The \setbox/\cleaders approach may use more dvi output bytes per item, affecting I/O time. Balance computation vs memory vs I/O costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate efficiency considering dvi output size and I/O costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some methods generate more dvi bytes per produced element (e.g., setbox/cleaders generates four bytes per asterisk vs one byte for other methods), so I/O time can dominate overall performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When optimizing macros, consider not only CPU time but also the size of generated dvi and the ensuing I/O/printing costs; a seemingly faster computation can be slower in practice due to larger I/O.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debug macro expansion with tracing options
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand TeX's expansion mechanism, watch it in action by looking at the log file with \tracingmacros=2 and \tracingcommands=2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tracing to see expansion order and diagnose problems caused by expansion vs assignment phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \expandafter and related tricks to control expansion order, but avoid excessive nesting
rubrics_metrics.description: The \expandafter primitive allows changing the expansion order (e.g., \expandafter\a\b expands \b before \a); repeated nesting can control several stages of expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While \expandafter chains are powerful, very long sequences are unwieldy and usually unnecessary; prefer clearer alternatives when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token-list membership/substring tests are level-sensitive and must account for grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple token-list tests (examples \atest and \btest) can detect whether a token (e.g., asterisk) appears at nesting level zero, because token-list registers are always balanced; asterisks inside groups ('hidden') won't be found by those tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to consider tokens at all nesting levels, use a slower routine built with \afterassignment that examines tokens one by one. Be mindful of the tradeoff between correctness across nesting and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space tokens and 'funny spaces' require special handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit and explicit space tokens may behave differently; \uppercase and \uccode can create 'funny space' tokens that are nearly identical to normal spaces but have distinct origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized lookahead macros like \futurenonspacelet to skip implicit/explicit spaces when scanning for following tokens. Distinguishing explicit vs implicit spaces is tricky; tests like \ifcat and \if comparisons and careful use of \uccode/\uppercase are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress unwanted expansion in \write arguments carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument to \write is expanded at \shipout; to prevent expansion, insert \noexpand before each control sequence or active character (example macro \unexpandedwrite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provided \unexpandedwrite assumes the tokens to be written do not include implicit spaces or braces and relies heavily on \aftergroup, so the parameter #2 should not include more than about 150 tokens. Respect these limitations or adapt a safer approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: List-macro conventions for storing and manipulating balanced items
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent lists as \{(item1)}\{(item2)}... (a parameterless control sequence expanding to such a sequence). Provide operations to left-append, right-append, concatenate, lop (remove leftmost), select by index, count cardinality, and center-list items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \leftappenditem, \rightappenditem, \concatenate, \lop, \cardinality, \select. Use \ifx\list\empty to test for emptiness. Running time of these operations is proportional to list length (efficient). Deleting the rightmost item in full generality in O(n) without extra tricks is not possible unless items are restricted (e.g., to unexpandable tokens) or \aftergroup trick is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unordered sets of control sequences via list macros and provide membership/removal operations
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'set macro' can be represented as \{\alpha\beta\gamma} and tested for membership via a macro that scans items (example \ismember).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient but slightly intricate constructions can remove all occurrences equivalent to a given control sequence; care is required when items are control words rather than simple tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \dospecials and uncatcoding to produce verbatim listings safely
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX's \dospecials lists characters with special catcodes, so defining a macro to set those characters to category 12 (other) allows verbatim printing of a file's characters and spacing (example \uncatcodespecials and \listing macros).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrap verbatim setup and \input inside a group (\begingroup ... \endgroup) so that \endgroup restores normal catcodes. Be aware that \input used inside the listing macro expands before verbatim setup if not carefully grouped; the provided \listing implementation ensures correct ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert count registers to and from control-sequence decimal representations
rubrics_metrics.description:
Convert a count register 
 to a control sequence holding its decimal expansion via \edef\csn{	he
}; conversely, assign back with 
=\csn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing such control-sequence-number for zero can be done with \if0\csn{true text}\else{false text}\fi because extra digits are ignored in number scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve conventional naming (caret vs circumflex/hat) for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The ASCII character appearing in position '186 is sometimes called 'caret' but dictionaries call the larger symbol a caret; the correct name for '^^' is 'circumflex' and a shorter name like 'hat' is preferable. Preserve the distinction between caret and hat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent terminology in macro/package documentation and code to avoid confusion across implementations and users.
